summary: Paints for walls, wood and other surfaces, waterproofing products, painting services and home furnishings, alongside industrial and overseas paint businesses.
description: Asian Paints makes paint and related products and supplies shops or business buyers. For example, a household repainting a bedroom needs paint, surface preparation and someone to apply it. A factory buying a protective coating has a different job to do. The company also offers painting and home-improvement services.
money: Buyers pay for paint, other products or agreed services. The company pays for ingredients, tins and packaging, factories, transport, advertising and staff. A painting or fitted-home service also needs people to complete the work. Profit depends on the amount left after the relevant costs and tax.
customers: Dealers and other businesses buying products to sell onward, households, painters, builders and industrial customers. The shop buying paint from Asian Paints can be a different customer from the household eventually using it.
drivers: How much paint people need, which ranges they choose, selling prices, ingredient and transport costs, shop availability and the cost of running factories and services.

groups.title: Wall paints
groups.explanation: Customers choose different finishes and prices for different surfaces. Coverage means how much area the paint can cover under stated conditions; preparing the wall and applying the paint also affect the result.

groups.title: Preparing and protecting surfaces
groups.examples: SmartCare waterproofing, primers, putty and WoodTech finishes.
groups.explanation: Primer helps prepare a surface before painting; putty helps smooth it. Waterproofing addresses water entry, while wood finishes protect or change the appearance of wood. These are different jobs, not simply more paint colours.

groups.title: Painting and home-improvement services
groups.examples: Beautiful Homes services and kitchen, bath, furnishing and lighting offerings.
groups.explanation: A customer can pay for work or fitted products as well as materials. Staff or partners must measure, arrange materials and finish the promised job; sending a paint tin is only one part of that service.

groups.title: Factory coatings and overseas paints
groups.examples: Automotive and other industrial coatings, plus overseas paint operations.
groups.explanation: A business buyer may need a coating that meets a technical requirement. Read which company supplies it: overseas companies and joint arrangements are not all the same as the Indian parent business.

basics.title: An existing home can create paint demand too
basics.text: A household may repaint an old room without building anything new. New construction and repainting are therefore different sources of demand. For a repainting example, the customer may need wall preparation, paint and labour, not a new house.

steps.title: Make the right type of paint
steps.text: Choose colouring ingredients, ingredients that hold the coating together and suitable packaging for the intended surface.

steps.title: Produce it and send it to buyers
steps.text: Factories make consistent products and supply dealers or business customers with the required ranges and colours.

steps.title: Help turn the product into a finished job
steps.text: Customers choose a colour and finish, and a painter or service team applies it. For contracted services, the agreed work must be completed.

steps.title: Receive payment and cover the costs
steps.text: Product buyers and service customers pay under their arrangements. Materials, factories, transport, people and any repairs or repeated work have to be paid for.

specifics.title: Paint in a dealer’s shop is not yet paint on a wall
specifics.text: Supplying more shops improves availability. It does not prove that final users bought and used all the paint sent there.

specifics.title: More litres can still bring less money
specifics.text: If prices fall or buyers choose cheaper ranges, more paint sold need not produce the same growth in sales value. Cheaper ingredients may also lead to lower customer prices.

specifics.title: A new factory and a kitchen service need different checks
specifics.text: A factory must sell enough paint to cover its costs. A fitted kitchen or painting service must finish jobs well and cover materials and labour. An opening announcement alone proves neither.

watch: Are people buying more paint or choosing different ranges?
Litres sold and money received can move differently.
Compare the company’s quantity and sales-value measures for the same business and period. Read price changes and cheaper versus premium ranges alongside them.
A dealer order can come before a household purchase.
Read dealer-stock and demand commentary. Check whether products are waiting longer in shops or customers owe more money; do not assume company shipments equal paint applied.
Who benefits when ingredients become cheaper?
Savings may be kept, or passed to customers through lower prices.
Compare ingredient costs, price cuts, discounts and profit commentary. Competition can make the company spend some of those savings to keep buyers.
Do new factories and home services cover their costs?
Both need money before enough sales arrive.
Follow factory opening and actual production, and read home-service or décor results separately. Check which company owns or operates the activity before comparing results.
Stock and unpaid customer bills can absorb money.
Read cash generated by day-to-day operations, unsold products, customer bills still unpaid and amounts owed to suppliers. Separate these from spending on factories or acquisitions.
risks: Discounts and payments to support dealer sales can reduce profit even if more litres are sold.
Some materials depend on commodity prices or imports; costs can rise before customer prices change.
Late work, poor application or faulty installation can lead to complaints, repeated work and extra costs.
New factories or ranges attract too little demand
Staff, buildings and equipment still cost money when sales grow slowly.
context: Price increases can make sales grow faster than litres

Asian Paints’ 29 October 2026 results presentation says its decorative business in India, meaning paints for homes and buildings, sold more paint by volume in July–September 2026. Its sales value grew faster because the company had raised prices after the cost of its ingredients rose sharply earlier in the year. Paint made with ingredients bought at those higher costs was still being sold, so gross margin, the share of sales left after paying for materials, fell. Group profit grew more slowly than sales. The same presentation says the first stage of a new plant at Dahej in Gujarat has started making VAE emulsion, a liquid ingredient used in its paint formulas, which the company would otherwise have to buy. The company expects a stronger cost benefit only after a second stage is running, so a plant start does not yet prove a saving.
quiz: Does selling more litres of paint guarantee more profit?
No. Selling prices, the ranges bought, ingredient costs, dealer incentives and factory or service costs also change what remains.
sources: Volume versus value, ingredient costs and Dahej plant · results presentation 29 October 2026

financialNotes.title: Check the business boundary before comparing
financialNotes.text: The audited group reports one business segment. The table shows revenue from operations and group profit after tax, including non-controlling interests. Decorative paints, industrial ventures, international activities and home décor are not assigned invented separate profits. Check how each venture enters the group accounts before comparing business highlights.
